Connection Title: Bacterial toxins that raise host-cell cAMP
Explanation: Cholera and ETEC LT sustain Gs signaling; pertussis toxin inhibits Gi signaling; anthrax edema factor is a calmodulin-dependent adenylate cyclase. Each raises cAMP through a different route.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Toxins increasing cAMP; cAMP-elevating exotoxins
Source Section: Bacterial Toxins, Exotoxin (p. 21); E. coli variants (p. 68); Vibrio (p. 87); Bordetella (p. 98); B. anthracis (p. 40)
Notes: Four distinct cAMP-elevating mechanisms verified. Correctly excludes ETEC heat-stable toxin (raises cGMP) and anthrax lethal factor (a MAPKK protease). Added refs: Dal Molin et al., BBRC 2008 (PMID 18793614); Tang & Guo, Mol Aspects Med 2009 (PMID 19560485).

Connection Title: Bacterial toxins that inhibit host protein synthesis
Explanation: Diphtheria toxin and exotoxin A ADP-ribosylate and inactivate elongation factor 2; Shiga toxin and Shiga-like toxin are N-glycosidases that cleave an adenine from 28S rRNA of the 60S subunit. All interrupt eukaryotic protein synthesis.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Exotoxins blocking eukaryotic translation; Protein-synthesis-inhibiting bacterial toxins
Source Section: Exotoxin (p. 21); C. diphtheriae (p. 60); EHEC (p. 68); Shigella (p. 74); Pseudomonas (p. 80)
Notes: Tiles 3-4 disambiguated by organism so all four are distinct toxins; Shiga (S. dysenteriae) and Shiga-like/Stx (EHEC) are mechanistically identical but genetically/organismally distinct. BOARD WARNING: near-identical Shiga pair can feel easy. Refs: Cherubin et al., Sci Rep 2018; Perentesis, BioFactors 1992 (PMID 1599611); Menge, Toxins 2020 (PMID 32456125); Freedman, NEJM 2023.

Connection Title: Classic toxins associated with lysogenic conversion
Explanation: Toxin-producing strains acquire these virulence genes through bacteriophage (prophage) carriage rather than all strains of a species inherently producing the toxin: diphtheria (corynephage beta), cholera (CTX-phi), SpeA (phage T12), and Shiga-like toxin (lambdoid prophage).
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Phage-encoded virulence toxins; Toxins acquired through lysogenic conversion
Source Section: Bacterial Genetics, Transduction (p. 15); C. diphtheriae (p. 60); GAS (p. 33); EHEC (p. 68)
Notes: Phage-encoded (lysogenic conversion) toxins verified (ABCD'S set). Not all strains carry the prophage. Refs: Bruessow et al., MMBR 2004 (PMID 15353570); Arnold & Koudelka, Environ Microbiol 2014; Jariah & Hakim, Rev Med Virol 2019.

Explanation: These organisms secrete IgA1 protease to cleave the hinge of mucosal IgA1 and aid colonization. This is a virulence association, not a claim that all strains express identical enzyme activity.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: IgA-cleaving bacteria; Mucosal pathogens producing IgA protease; SHiN organisms
Notes: SHiN IgA1-protease producers verified. Refs: Mulks et al., J Infect Dis 1980 (PMID 6989925); Kilian et al., J Immunol 1980 (PMID 6768797); Bender & Weiser, Mol Microbiol 2006.

Explanation: Each is a clinically important anaerobic, endospore-forming gram-positive bacillus. Clostridioides difficile retains these phenotypic properties despite its genus reassignment.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Anaerobic endospore-forming rods; Classic clostridial spore formers
Notes: Phenotype verified. Competing 'clostridial toxin-mediated disease' category overlaps all four; resolve at board assembly. Ref: Murray, Medical Microbiology 9e.

Explanation: These organisms hydrolyze urea. In urinary pathogens this can alkalinize urine and promote struvite stones; H. pylori uses urease in its gastric niche. Urease positivity does not imply identical diseases or equal stone risk.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Bacteria producing urease; Urea-hydrolyzing pathogens
Source Section: S. saprophyticus (p. 27); Klebsiella (p. 69); Proteus (p. 79); H. pylori (p. 86)
Notes: Urease positivity verified. Three urinary + one gastric organism make the enzyme the coherent link. Ref: Murray 9e; Jawetz/Melnick & Adelberg 28e.

Explanation: Fastidious or intracellular organisms classically implicated in culture-negative endocarditis. Coxiella, Bartonella, and Brucella are true culture-negative causes requiring serology/PCR; HACEK (incl. Haemophilus) is fastidious but is now usually recoverable in modern automated systems with >=5-day incubation.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Fastidious endocarditis pathogens; Organisms considered in culture-negative endocarditis
Notes: Explanation revised: HACEK now typically grows in modern blood cultures, so 'fastidious/historically culture-negative' is accurate rather than 'invariably negative.' Tropheryma whipplei is an independently supported alternate member for a stricter true-culture-negative set. Refs: Li et al., Lancet 2024; AHA/IDSA (Baddour) 2015; Holland et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016; Chambers & Bayer, NEJM 2020.

Connection Title: Classic bacterial causes of atypical pneumonia
Explanation: These cause pneumonia classically grouped as atypical; exposure clues and extrapulmonary findings distinguish them. The category does not require identical radiographic appearances.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Atypical bacterial pneumonia pathogens; Classic walking-pneumonia differential
Notes: Verified; Coxiella is an additional source-listed atypical cause. Chlamydophila nomenclature accepted. Ref: Murray 9e; Jawetz 28e.

Connection Title: Bacterial infections linked to unpasteurized dairy
Explanation: Each is associated with unpasteurized dairy exposure. Resulting syndromes differ; this exposure is one recognized transmission route rather than the only route.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Unpasteurized-milk bacterial infections; Raw-dairy pathogen exposures
Notes: Verified. EHEC, M. bovis, and Coxiella share the raw-dairy route; assess overlap at board assembly. Ref: Holland et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016 (Brucella/dairy); CDC.

Connection Title: Implanted sites classically infected by S. epidermidis
Explanation: S. epidermidis adheres to foreign surfaces and forms biofilm, making these implanted devices/prostheses characteristic infection sites. Device infection can also be caused by other organisms.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: S. epidermidis foreign-body infections; Device-associated staphylococcal biofilm sites
Notes: Tile 4 'Cardiac implanted device' replaced with 'Prosthetic joint': original was non-distinct from Tile 1 (prosthetic valve is a cardiac implant). CoNS/S. epidermidis is the most common cause of prosthetic joint infection and biofilm device infection. Refs: Patel, NEJM 2023; Boyle et al., Curr Rev Musculoskelet Med 2018; Heilmann et al., Clin Microbiol Infect 2019; Santos et al., Sci Rep 2025.

Explanation: Tetanospasmin blocks inhibitory neurotransmitter release, producing rigidity and sustained spasms including these findings. Individual findings need not all be present.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Tetanus-associated muscular findings; Findings from loss of inhibitory neurotransmission
Source Section: Clostridium Tetani (p. 47); Infectious Spinal Cord Disease (p. 262)
Notes: Verified. Ref: Murray 9e; CDC Tetanus.

Explanation: Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release. Somatic neuromuscular blockade causes flaccid weakness and reduced reflexes; autonomic cholinergic blockade causes dilated pupils and dry mouth.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Botulinum-toxin clinical findings; Somatic and autonomic features of botulism
Source Section: Clostridium Botulinum (p. 48); Infectious Spinal Cord Disease (p. 262)
Notes: Verified; autonomic findings strengthen specificity vs other neuromuscular disorders. Ref: Murray 9e; CDC Botulism.

Explanation: Legionella pneumonia may follow contaminated-water aerosol exposure and feature hyponatremia and GI symptoms. Urine antigen testing is a useful clue but mainly detects L. pneumophila serogroup 1.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Legionella pneumonia clues; Legionnaires disease associations
Notes: Verified; symptoms/sodium are associations, not required criteria; retain urine-antigen serogroup limitation. Ref: Murray 9e; CDC Legionella.

Explanation: P. aeruginosa is classically linked to these syndromes via wet environments, diabetes/immunocompromise, contact lenses, and plantar puncture wounds. These syndromes are not all exclusively pseudomonal.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Classic Pseudomonas clinical associations; Exposure clues to P. aeruginosa
Notes: Verified; other bacteria can cause corneal ulcers/wound infections. Ref: Murray 9e.

Explanation: Characteristic late manifestations of congenital syphilis reflecting developmental and tissue injury. These are not the Hutchinson triad, which comprises Hutchinson teeth, interstitial keratitis, and eighth-nerve deafness.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Late congenital Treponema pallidum findings; Congenital syphilis stigmata
Notes: Verified; keep 'late congenital' wording; do not label this four-tile set a triad. Ref: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021.

Explanation: These four findings form the Amsel framework for bacterial vaginosis. Clinical diagnosis requires at least three of the four, not all four.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Amsel criteria; Bacterial-vaginosis bedside findings
Notes: Amsel criteria and the 3-of-4 rule independently confirmed. Refs: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021 (Workowski); ACOG Vaginitis 2020; Leclair & Stenson, JAMA 2022.

Explanation: These endemic dimorphic fungi commonly establish infection after inhaled environmental propagules. Coccidioides forms tissue spherules rather than budding yeast; Sporothrix is omitted because its classic route is traumatic inoculation.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Inhaled endemic dimorphic mycoses; Endemic pulmonary dimorphic fungi
Notes: Verified; do not impose yeast-in-tissue wording on Coccidioides. BOARD WARNING: shares 3 members (Histo/Blasto/Paracocci) with MICRO-019 - do not place both on one 16-tile board. Refs: Munoz et al., Sci Rep 2018; Gauthier, Mediators Inflamm 2016; Thompson et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2021 (ECMM/ISHAM).

Connection Title: Tissue forms of dimorphic fungi that become yeast
Explanation: These fungi are molds in the environment and yeast in mammalian tissue, differing in budding pattern and shape. Coccidioides is excluded because it forms spherules in tissue.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Mold in the cold and yeast in tissue; Yeast tissue phase of classic dimorphic fungi
Notes: Verified. BOARD WARNING: shares 3 members with MICRO-018 (different defining concept and 4th member). Refs: Boyce & Andrianopoulos, FEMS Microbiol Rev 2015 (PMID 26253139); Munoz et al., Sci Rep 2018; Gauthier 2016.

Explanation: Cryptococcus has a prominent polysaccharide capsule demonstrable by these stains or by antigen assay (which detects capsular polysaccharide, glucuronoxylomannan); CNS infection can produce gelatinous pseudocysts. Imaging findings are neither required nor exclusive.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Cryptococcal meningitis diagnostic associations; Encapsulated yeast diagnostic clues
Notes: Explanation corrected: cryptococcal antigen detects capsular POLYSACCHARIDE, not a protein (original source error). India ink is less sensitive than antigen testing. All four tiles valid. Ref: Murray 9e; IDSA Cryptococcosis guideline.

Explanation: Invasive Aspergillus infection can yield septate acute-angle branching hyphae, galactomannan positivity, pulmonary nodules/cavitation, and bleeding from tissue/vascular invasion. No single clue is fully specific.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Invasive Aspergillus diagnostic features; Invasive aspergillosis associations
Notes: Verified; positive galactomannan is not definitive alone and other molds can cause nodules/bleeding. Ref: Murray 9e.

Explanation: ABPA is a hypersensitivity syndrome associated with asthma or cystic fibrosis, elevated IgE, eosinophilia, and (often central) bronchiectasis. These are characteristic associations rather than a complete diagnostic checklist.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: ABPA clinical associations; Aspergillus hypersensitivity in airways
Notes: Verified; bronchiectasis is not mandatory in every ABPA phenotype - avoid universal wording. Ref: Murray 9e.

Explanation: Mucorales infection is classically associated with DKA and necrotic sinus/palatal disease extending into orbit and brain. Histology shows broad pauciseptate hyphae with wide, irregular branching.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Mucormycosis diagnostic constellation; Invasive Mucorales clues
Notes: Verified; 'pauciseptate' (not absolutely nonseptate) and variable branching angle retained. Ref: Murray 9e.

Explanation: Candida can cause these mucosal or superficial skin infections. Esophageal disease carries different immune-risk and treatment implications from uncomplicated oral, vaginal, or skin infection.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Mucosal and superficial Candida infections; Candidiasis at epithelial sites
Notes: Verified; esophageal candidiasis is AIDS-defining/deeper, and vulvovaginal disease need not indicate immunodeficiency. Ref: Murray 9e; HHS OI Guidelines 2026.

Explanation: P. jirovecii pneumonia is a key opportunistic infection in advanced HIV, causing subacute exertional dyspnea and diffuse ground-glass opacities. TMP-SMX is the classic prophylactic agent in appropriate patients.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: PJP high-yield associations; Pneumocystis clinical and prevention clues
Notes: Verified; CD4<200 is a teaching threshold, not the complete prophylaxis algorithm. Ref: HHS OI Guidelines 2026.

Explanation: Invasive E. histolytica can cause colonic ulceration and spread to the liver. Erythrophagocytosis supports pathogenic amoebae; characteristic abscess material is a classic association, not a reason for routine aspiration.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Invasive amebiasis diagnostic clues; Amebic colitis and liver-abscess associations
Notes: Verified; do not imply every amebic liver abscess requires drainage. Ref: CDC DPDx Entamoeba.

Explanation: Giardia can follow contaminated-water ingestion, cause nonbloody malabsorptive diarrhea, and be more troublesome with IgA deficiency. Trophozoites have a characteristic paired-nuclear appearance.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Giardia associations; Malabsorptive protozoal-diarrhea clues
Notes: Verified; clues support suspicion and require confirmatory testing. Ref: CDC DPDx Giardia.

Tile 3: Chronic watery diarrhea in advanced HIV
Explanation: Cryptosporidium is acquired by ingesting oocysts and may cause severe persistent watery diarrhea with impaired cellular immunity. Modified acid-fast oocysts support diagnosis; immune restoration is central to HIV-associated disease.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Cryptosporidium diagnostic and host clues; HIV-associated cryptosporidiosis
Notes: Verified; distinguish modified acid-fast from molecular/antigen assays; ART is not an immediate cure. Ref: CDC DPDx; HHS OI Guidelines 2026.

Explanation: Chronic T. cruzi infection can injure myocardium and the enteric nervous system, producing cardiomyopathy, rhythm disturbances, and dilation of the esophagus or colon. Many infected people remain asymptomatic.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Chronic Trypanosoma cruzi complications; Cardiac and digestive Chagas disease
Notes: Verified; 'can cause' retained - digestive disease frequency varies geographically. Ref: CDC Chagas disease.

Explanation: These four traditional board-focused Plasmodium species differ in severity, erythrocyte preference, fever periodicity, and liver-stage persistence. This is a classic teaching set, not an exhaustive list of human malaria species.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Traditional human Plasmodium species; Classic malaria-causing species
Notes: Verified; 'classic' qualifier retained because P. knowlesi is a recognized fifth human species. Do not confuse hypnozoites (vivax/ovale) with schizonts. Ref: CDC DPDx Malaria.

Explanation: Babesia infects red cells and can cause hemolysis; tetrads may appear as Maltese crosses. Ixodes exposure is classic for B. microti, and absent splenic function increases risk of severe disease.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Babesia clinical associations; Tick-borne erythrocyte-parasite clues
Notes: Verified; Maltese crosses are not on every smear and transfusion transmission occurs. Ref: CDC DPDx Babesia.

Explanation: Visceral Leishmania is transmitted by sandflies and involves reticuloendothelial macrophages. Organ enlargement and cytopenias are characteristic; tissue examination reveals amastigotes.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Kala-azar clues; Visceral Leishmania host and tissue findings
Notes: Verified; do not imply a single sandfly species transmits all Leishmania worldwide. Ref: CDC DPDx Leishmania.

Connection Title: Nematodes with a pulmonary migration phase
Explanation: Larvae of these intestinal nematodes pass through the lungs before reaching or returning to the intestine. Pulmonary migration can cause cough or eosinophilic inflammation but need not be symptomatic.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Intestinal worms with lung migration; Larval lung-phase nematodes
Notes: Verified (Loeffler syndrome worms); two hookworm species are distinct genera. Competing category: eosinophilic pulmonary syndromes. Do not conflate with animal-hookworm cutaneous larva migrans. Ref: CDC DPDx.

Connection Title: Nematodes acquired by ingestion of eggs
Explanation: These nematodes infect humans after eggs are ingested. Toxocara remains a larval tissue infection in humans (visceral larva migrans), while the other three mature as intestinal worms. Eggs differ in environmental maturation requirements.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Egg-ingestion nematodes; Nematode infections from swallowed infective eggs
Notes: Verified; infective-egg stage is the specific link vs broad fecal-oral exposure. Ref: CDC DPDx.

Connection Title: Parasites acquired through infected meat or fish larvae
Explanation: Ingestion of larvae in infected pork, beef, game meat, or freshwater fish causes intestinal taeniasis, trichinellosis, or fish-tapeworm infection. T. solium EGG ingestion (not pork cysticerci) causes cysticercosis.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Foodborne larval helminth infections; Meat-and-fish larval parasite transmission
Notes: Verified; taeniasis-vs-cysticercosis distinction preserved. Dibothriocephalus latus = updated name for Diphyllobothrium latum (accepted older synonym). Clonorchis is another foodborne larval parasite not in this subset. Ref: CDC DPDx.

Connection Title: Hydatid disease diagnostic and complication clues
Explanation: Echinococcus granulosus cycles between canine definitive hosts and intermediate hosts such as sheep. Humans ingest eggs and may develop hepatic cysts; rupture can provoke severe allergic reactions. Calcification is possible, not universal.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Cystic echinococcosis associations; Echinococcus granulosus clues
Notes: Verified; avoid unplanned biopsy/aspiration. Ref: CDC Echinococcosis; WHO-IWGE guidance.

Explanation: Praziquantel treats these trematode and cestode infections. The category specifies intestinal taeniasis rather than assuming identical regimens for neurocysticercosis.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Praziquantel-susceptible helminth infections; Fluke-and-tapeworm uses of praziquantel
Notes: Verified; retain intestinal-taeniasis qualifier (neurocysticercosis management differs). Ref: Katzung 15e; CDC Parasites treatment.

Connection Title: Parasite infections with ivermectin treatment options
Explanation: Ivermectin has treatment roles in these nematode and ectoparasite infections. Route, patient factors, contraindications, and alternative drugs differ across indications.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Ivermectin indications; Nematode and ectoparasite uses of ivermectin
Notes: Verified; head lice may be treated with FDA-approved topical ivermectin or off-label oral ivermectin, not interchangeable first-line; screen for Loa loa co-infection before onchocerciasis/filarial treatment. Ref: Katzung 15e; FDA ivermectin and Sklice labels.

Explanation: These viruses have recognized Aedes mosquito transmission. Zika also has sexual and vertical routes; yellow fever has additional sylvatic mosquito cycles. The title does not claim exclusive Aedes transmission.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Viruses spread by Aedes mosquitoes; Aedes-associated arboviruses
Source Section: Flaviviridae (p. 195); Yellow Fever (p. 197); Zika (p. 198); Dengue (p. 199); Chikungunya (p. 204)
Notes: Verified; 'has Aedes transmission' wording retained. Ref: CDC Arboviral diseases.

Explanation: These groups have segmented RNA genomes that permit reassortment. Rotavirus has 11 double-stranded RNA segments; influenza A/B have 8; arenaviruses have 2 (ambisense); traditional bunyavirus groups have 3 negative-sense/ambisense segments.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Segmented RNA viruses; RNA viruses capable of genome reassortment
Notes: Taxonomy/segment counts corrected in explanation; 'Bunyavirus groups' updated to order Bunyavirales. Mixed abstraction (families vs rotavirus genus) retained but flagged for tile-level fairness. Refs: McDonald et al., Nat Rev Microbiol 2016 (PMID 27211789); Weber & Weber, Curr Opin Microbiol 2014 (PMID 24930021).

Explanation: Their fusion (F) proteins mediate fusion of the viral envelope with host membranes and can drive syncytium formation between infected cells. RSV is now classified in Pneumoviridae rather than Paramyxoviridae.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: F-protein respiratory viruses; Viruses causing syncytia through fusion proteins
Source Section: Paramyxoviridae Overview (p. 215); Parainfluenza (p. 216); RSV (p. 217); Mumps (p. 218); Measles (p. 219)
Notes: Verified; do not label all four current Paramyxoviridae (RSV is Pneumoviridae). Competing structural category: enveloped negative-sense respiratory RNA viruses. Ref: Murray 9e.

Explanation: These lack a lipid envelope. Parvovirus B19 has a single-stranded DNA genome; the others have double-stranded DNA. They should not be grouped as sharing the same strand number or genome shape.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Nonenveloped DNA viruses; DNA viruses without a lipid envelope
Notes: Verified (Parvo/Adeno/Papilloma/Polyoma); classic structural teaching set, not every nonenveloped DNA virus. Ref: Murray 9e.

Explanation: These IARC-recognized high-risk types are associated with epithelial dysplasia and cancers via E6/E7 effects on tumor-suppressor pathways. They are not the complete list of high-risk HPV types.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: High-risk HPV genotypes; Oncogenic HPV strains
Notes: Verified; IARC Group 1 carcinogenic types include 16,18,31,33,35,39,45,51,52,56,58,59. Avoid implying only these four are oncogenic or that infection inevitably causes cancer. Refs: Perkins et al., JAMA 2023; Massad et al., ASCCP 2025.

Explanation: High-risk HPV contributes to squamous carcinomas at these sites. The attributable proportion differs by site, and HPV-negative carcinomas also occur.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Sites of HPV-associated SCC; Squamous malignancies linked to high-risk HPV
Notes: Verified; preserve squamous histology/oropharyngeal wording (not all head-and-neck cancer). Refs: Spurgeon, J Virol 2026; HHS OI Guidelines 2026.

Explanation: EBV is strongly linked to endemic Burkitt lymphoma and AIDS-associated primary CNS lymphoma and to subsets of Hodgkin lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Qualifiers prevent treating all tumors in these classes as EBV-caused.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Malignancies associated with Epstein-Barr virus; EBV-associated cancers
Notes: Verified with geographic/histologic qualifiers; nasopharyngeal carcinoma makes EBV the coherent four-member link. Ref: Murray 9e.

Connection Title: Organ disease from CMV in immunosuppression
Explanation: CMV reactivation can produce these end-organ diseases when cellular immunity is impaired. Retinitis is classic at very low CD4 counts; CMV esophagitis causes deep/linear ulcers; pneumonitis is especially relevant after transplantation.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: CMV end-organ disease; Opportunistic cytomegalovirus syndromes
Notes: Verified; CMV linear/deep ulcers contrast with HSV punched-out ulcers; presentations alone are not diagnostic of CMV. Ref: HHS OI Guidelines 2026.

Explanation: Congenital CMV can produce this neurologic and sensory constellation. PERIventricular calcifications help distinguish it from the more diffuse intracranial calcifications of congenital toxoplasmosis.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Congenital cytomegalovirus associations; Classic congenital CMV sequelae
Notes: Verified; calcification distribution distinguishes CMV from other congenital infections (Zika, toxoplasmosis). Ref: Murray 9e; CDC Congenital CMV.

Explanation: Congenital rubella has a classic cardiac-ocular-auditory triad (PDA, cataracts, deafness), with dermal extramedullary hematopoiesis sometimes producing a blueberry-muffin rash. The rash is not rubella-specific.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Congenital rubella syndrome findings; Rubella embryopathy associations
Notes: Verified; these are four associated findings, not a four-part triad. Blueberry-muffin rash/deafness overlap congenital CMV; PDA and cataracts favor rubella. Ref: CDC Rubella.

Explanation: B19 can cause childhood exanthem and adult arthropathy; suppression of erythroid precursors causes aplastic crisis in high-turnover states and fetal anemia with hydrops after transplacental infection.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Clinical consequences of parvovirus B19; B19 rash-joint-marrow-fetal syndromes
Notes: Verified; aplastic crisis requires underlying high RBC turnover; hydrops is possible, not inevitable. Ref: Murray 9e.

Explanation: Recognized extrahepatic HCV associations. Mixed cryoglobulinemia can mediate glomerular injury; dermatologic associations vary in strength and are not exclusive to HCV.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Extrahepatic HCV manifestations; Renal and skin associations of chronic HCV
Notes: Verified; cryoglobulinemia and MPGN are mechanistically linked (not fully independent). Preserve association language for PCT/lichen planus. Ref: Murray 9e; AASLD-IDSA HCV guidance.

Connection Title: Mumps complications outside the parotid gland
Explanation: Mumps can involve gonadal, pancreatic, and neural tissues, producing these complications. They are possible outcomes, not required features or inevitable causes of infertility.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Extraglandular mumps complications; Systemic complications of mumps
Notes: Verified; orchitis mainly post-pubertal; permanent infertility is not universal. Ref: CDC Mumps.

Explanation: These diseases are caused by members of Poxviridae, large complex DNA viruses that replicate in the cytoplasm. The four are distinct diseases, not synonyms for one virus.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Human poxvirus-associated diseases; Poxviridae clinical illnesses
Notes: Verified; smallpox eradicated - category describes causation/virology, not prevalence. Ref: CDC; Murray 9e.

Explanation: Classic peripheral findings that can accompany infective endocarditis through vascular/embolic or immune-mediated phenomena. Their absence does not exclude endocarditis, and none is fully specific.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Peripheral stigmata of infective endocarditis; Endocarditis vascular and immune findings
Notes: Verified; mix of immune (Osler nodes, Roth spots) and vascular/embolic (Janeway lesions, splinter hemorrhages) phenomena - do not label all four one type. Refs: Chambers & Bayer, NEJM 2020; AHA/IDSA 2015.

Explanation: These penicillins resist staphylococcal penicillinase and target susceptible staphylococci. Methicillin is mainly a historical/laboratory reference; altered PBP2a in MRSA defeats the class.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Antistaphylococcal penicillins; Penicillinase-stable penicillins
Notes: Verified; methicillin is not a routine current prescribing option and the class is not MRSA therapy. Ref: Katzung 15e.

Explanation: These beta-lactams inhibit bacterial cell-wall crosslinking by binding PBPs. Ertapenem lacks reliable Pseudomonas activity, and imipenem is given with cilastatin.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Carbapenem beta-lactams; Carbapenem PBP inhibitors
Notes: Verified; retain ertapenem antipseudomonal exception. Ref: Katzung 15e.

Explanation: These third-generation cephalosporins bind PBPs and inhibit cell-wall synthesis. Spectrum and route vary; only ceftazidime among these has meaningful antipseudomonal activity.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Third-generation cephalosporin antibiotics; Generation-three cephalosporins
Notes: Verified; do not imply all four cover Pseudomonas or are interchangeable for meningitis. Ref: Katzung 15e.

Connection Title: Antibiotic groups acting on the 50S ribosome
Explanation: These agents/classes inhibit bacterial translation at the 50S subunit, with differing effects on translocation, initiation, or peptidyl transfer. The shared subunit does not mean an identical binding site.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: 50S-targeting antibacterial agents; Bacterial large-subunit translation inhibitors
Notes: Verified; note mixed abstraction (macrolides is a class; others are single drugs) - tile-level fairness. Do not call all four translocation inhibitors. Ref: Katzung 15e.

Explanation: These aminoglycosides act at the 30S ribosome and disrupt translation. Uptake requires oxygen-dependent transport; nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity are key class risks.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Aminoglycoside 30S inhibitors; Bactericidal aminoglycosides
Notes: Verified; competing adverse-effect category (nephrotoxic/ototoxic antibiotics) overlaps - treat as board-assembly overlap. Ref: Katzung 15e.

Explanation: These bind the 30S subunit and block aminoacyl-tRNA access. The class shares divalent-cation chelation and effects on developing teeth, with important differences in use and toxicity.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Tetracycline-class 30S inhibitors; Aminoacyl-tRNA binding blockers
Notes: Verified; avoid a blanket absolute pediatric/pregnancy contraindication - doxycycline has indication-specific exceptions (e.g., RMSF). Competing categories: chelated-by-cations / tooth-discoloration drugs. Ref: Katzung 15e; CDC RMSF.

Explanation: These fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase and/or topoisomerase IV. Their respiratory, urinary, anaerobic, and antipseudomonal spectra differ.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Fluoroquinolone antibiotics; Bacterial DNA-gyrase/topoisomerase IV inhibitors
Notes: Verified; preserve spectrum differences (moxifloxacin is not a reliable urinary/antipseudomonal agent). Competing adverse-effect category: tendon/aortic injury-risk antibiotics. Ref: Katzung 15e; FDA fluoroquinolone labels.

Explanation: These rifamycins inhibit bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Rifaximin is minimally absorbed with intestinal uses; CYP-enzyme induction varies between agents.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Bacterial transcription inhibitors; Rifamycin antibiotics
Notes: Verified; do not assign systemic TB therapy or equal CYP induction to every agent. Ref: Katzung 15e.

Explanation: These four drugs constitute the classic initial RIPE regimen for drug-susceptible active TB. Regimen and duration depend on susceptibility, site, patient factors, and current guidance.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: RIPE regimen; Classic initial four-drug tuberculosis treatment
Notes: Verified; 'classic initial' regimen for active drug-susceptible TB, not for latent TB. Ref: CDC/ATS/IDSA (Nahid et al.), Clin Infect Dis 2016.

Explanation: These triazoles inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (CYP51), impairing ergosterol synthesis. They differ in spectrum, pharmacokinetics, interactions, and adverse effects.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Ergosterol-synthesis-inhibiting triazoles; Fungal CYP51 inhibitors
Notes: Verified; do not generalize all azole toxicities/contraindications; isavuconazole is an additional member. Ref: Katzung 15e.

Explanation: These drugs have anti-CMV activity through distinct mechanisms: ganciclovir (viral-kinase-activated DNA-polymerase inhibitor), maribavir (UL97 kinase inhibitor), foscarnet (pyrophosphate analogue DNA-polymerase inhibitor), and cidofovir (nucleotide analogue DNA-polymerase inhibitor). Selection depends on toxicity, resistance, and indication.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Anti-CMV antiviral drugs; CMV-active antivirals
Notes: Tile 2 'Valganciclovir' replaced with 'Maribavir': valganciclovir is the valyl-ester prodrug of ganciclovir (same active moiety/mechanism/resistance), so not a distinct tile. Maribavir (FDA-approved for refractory/resistant CMV) gives four distinct agents. Alternate name revised (removed 'DNA-polymerase inhibitors' since maribavir targets UL97). Refs: FDA Livtencity (maribavir) label 2025; Imlay & Kaul, Clin Infect Dis 2021 (PMID 33197929); Hardinger & Brennan, Ann Pharmacother 2024.

Explanation: These antiretrovirals inhibit integrase-mediated incorporation of viral DNA into the host genome. They are used in combination regimens and differ in boosting and interaction requirements.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: INSTIs; HIV integrase inhibitors
Notes: Verified; avoid implying INSTI monotherapy is standard. Ref: HHS Adult/Adolescent ARV Guidelines; Katzung 15e.

Explanation: These bind HIV-1 reverse transcriptase allosterically and do not require phosphorylation. HIV-2 is intrinsically resistant to the class; agent-specific interaction/toxicity profiles differ.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: NNRTIs; Allosteric HIV reverse-transcriptase inhibitors
Notes: Verified; do not generalize older efavirenz pregnancy statements to the class. Ref: HHS Adult/Adolescent ARV Guidelines.

Explanation: These nucleoside analogues require intracellular phosphorylation and cause DNA-chain termination during reverse transcription. They differ in resistance, toxicity, and anti-HBV activity.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Nucleoside NRTIs; Nucleoside antiretroviral chain terminators
Notes: Verified; tenofovir (nucleotide analogue) intentionally excluded to keep tiles strictly nucleoside analogues. Ref: HHS Adult/Adolescent ARV Guidelines.

Explanation: These inhibit HIV protease and block polyprotein processing and virion maturation. Ritonavir is now mainly used at low dose as a pharmacokinetic booster but retains protease-inhibitor identity.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Antiretroviral protease inhibitors; HIV maturation-blocking protease inhibitors
Notes: Verified; do not infer all four are equally common current regimen components. Ref: HHS Adult/Adolescent ARV Guidelines.

Explanation: These target HCV NS5A, a protein involved in viral replication and assembly. They are used within direct-acting antiviral combinations rather than as interchangeable monotherapy.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Hepatitis C NS5A-targeted agents; NS5A direct-acting antivirals
Notes: Verified (-asvir class); genotype coverage/resistance requires separate review. Ref: AASLD-IDSA HCV Guidance.

Explanation: These inhibit HCV NS3/4A protease and impair viral protein processing. The grouping is mechanistic and includes both current and older agents, not a recommended regimen.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: HCV protease inhibitors; NS3/4A direct-acting antivirals
Notes: Verified (-previr class); avoid in decompensated (Child-Pugh B/C) cirrhosis. Ref: AASLD-IDSA HCV Guidance.
